title: Introduction to Max Flow / Min Cut
description: The theorem that the largest flow equals the smallest cut, and how to use it

sections.title: 4. The Max Flow Min Cut Theorem
12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: The max flow min cut theorem is one of the most beautiful results in all of graph theory. It says that the maximum flow you can push from a source to a sink is exactly equal to the capacity of the smallest cut separating them.

In other words, the most you can send equals the least you must destroy to cut the connection. This surprising equality links two problems that look completely different, and it powers a wide range of applications.

blocks.caption: A cut separates the source side from the sink side; its capacity bounds the flow
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762092-641818924.png

By the end of this topic you will understand what a cut is, what its capacity means, the theorem itself and why it holds, how to actually find the minimum cut, and the powerful problems it solves. It builds directly on network flow.

It is worth pausing on how strange this equality is. One problem is about pushing as much through the network as you can; the other is about the cheapest way to sever it. Yet their answers are identical.
That coincidence is not luck, it is a deep structural fact, and it is what makes the theorem so useful in practice.
Recall the setup from network flow. You have a directed graph with a capacity on each edge, a source, and a sink, and you want to push as much flow as possible from source to sink.

The maximum flow is limited by bottlenecks. Somewhere in the network, a set of edges forms the tightest barrier, and no matter how you route the flow, you cannot exceed the total capacity of that barrier. The min cut makes that idea precise.

items: A flow network has capacities, a source, and a sink
Max flow is the largest amount pushable from source to sink
Bottlenecks in the network limit the flow
The min cut formalises exactly what the bottleneck is

blocks.text: If you are rusty on augmenting paths and the residual graph, revisit the network flow topic first, since everything here rests on it.

items: Edges have capacities
One source and one sink
Max flow is the largest source to sink amount
Bottlenecks cap the achievable flow

blocks.text: A cut is a way of splitting all the nodes into two groups: one side that contains the source, and one side that contains the sink. Every node ends up on one side or the other.

blocks.caption: A cut partitions the nodes into a source side and a sink side
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762092-327334333.png
Think of it as drawing a line through the network that separates the source from the sink. There are many possible cuts, since you can put the in between nodes on either side.

items: Split all nodes into two sides
The source is on one side, the sink on the other
In between nodes can go on either side
Each such split is one possible cut

blocks.text: Because the in between nodes can each go on either side, a network with many nodes has an enormous number of possible cuts.
The theorem is about just one of them, the cheapest, which perfectly captures the bottleneck.

items: Every node lands on the source side or the sink side
The source is always on one side, the sink on the other
In between nodes may go on either side
Each assignment is a distinct cut

blocks.text: The capacity of a cut is the total capacity of the edges that cross from the source side to the sink side. Only the edges pointing forward across the cut count.

blocks.caption: The cut capacity is the total capacity of edges crossing from the source side to the sink side
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762092-818023223.png

Edges that go backward, from the sink side to the source side, do not add to the capacity. Intuitively, the cut capacity measures how much flow could possibly cross that dividing line in the forward direction.

Only forward crossings count:

When measuring a cut capacity, sum the capacities of edges from the source side to the sink side only. Backward edges are ignored.
Getting this direction right matters. A common error is to also add backward crossing edges, which inflates the capacity and breaks the theorem.

Direction is the trap:

Sum only the source side to sink side edges. Edges pointing the other way across the cut contribute nothing to its capacity.

content.title: 4. The Max Flow Min Cut Theorem

blocks.text: Now the centrepiece. The max flow min cut theorem states that the value of the maximum flow from source to sink is exactly equal to the capacity of the minimum cut.

blocks.caption: The maximum flow always equals the minimum cut capacity
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762093-88002155.png
blocks.alt: The Max Flow Min Cut Theorem

blocks.text: Every cut is an upper bound on the flow, because all flow from the source to the sink must cross that dividing line, and cannot exceed the total capacity crossing it. The theorem says the best flow reaches the tightest such bound exactly.

items: Any cut capacity is an upper bound on the flow
The minimum cut is the tightest such bound
The maximum flow equals that minimum cut capacity
So the two optimisation problems have the same answer

blocks.text: The upper bound half is easy to feel: every unit of flow must physically cross the dividing line, so the flow can never exceed the capacity crossing it.
The theorem sharpens that from an inequality into an exact equality, which is the surprising and powerful part.
The intuition comes in two halves. First, no flow can beat any cut, since everything going from source to sink must pass through the edges crossing that cut. So max flow is at most the min cut.

Second, when the augmenting path algorithm finishes, there is no path left from source to sink in the residual graph. The set of nodes still reachable from the source forms a cut, and every edge crossing it is completely saturated. That saturated cut has capacity exactly equal to the flow, so max flow is at least the min cut too.

Squeezed from both sides:

Flow can never exceed a cut, and the finished algorithm produces a cut equal to the flow. The only way both hold is if max flow equals min cut.
The saturated cut produced at the end is also a certificate. It proves the flow is optimal, because you can point to a barrier whose capacity the flow already fully uses.
This is why you never have to wonder whether Ford-Fulkerson stopped too early; the matching cut guarantees it did not.
So the flow can never beat a cut, and the algorithm always ends with a cut it exactly matches, which forces the two optima to be equal.
The theorem is not just elegant, it is constructive. Once you compute the maximum flow, the minimum cut falls out of the residual graph for free.

blocks.caption: After max flow, the nodes reachable from the source in the residual graph define the min cut
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762093-14645787.png

From the source, run a search over the residual graph, following only edges that still have spare capacity. The set of reachable nodes is the source side of a minimum cut, and the edges going from that set to the rest are the cut edges.
The reachable set from the source in the residual graph is exactly the source side of a minimum cut, and it costs only a single traversal to compute.
Remember to measure the cut edges using the original capacities, since the residual capacities of saturated edges are zero.
Max flow and min cut are a classic example of duality: two problems, one asking to maximise and the other to minimise, whose optimal values are guaranteed to be equal.

This kind of pairing appears throughout optimisation. Solving one problem automatically solves the other, and each gives a certificate that the other is optimal. The max flow proves the cut cannot be smaller, and the cut proves the flow cannot be larger.

items: Max flow is a maximisation problem
Min cut is a minimisation problem
Their optimal values are always equal
Each acts as a proof of the other optimality

blocks.text: Duality is a recurring theme in optimisation, and max flow min cut is its most intuitive example, expressed entirely in the concrete language of graphs.
Once you have seen it here, the same maximise equals minimise pattern becomes easier to recognise elsewhere.
In short, solving either problem hands you the solution to the other, along with a proof that it is optimal.

One striking use is separating an image into foreground and background. Each pixel becomes a node, and edges connect neighbouring pixels and connect pixels to a source and a sink representing the two labels.

Edge capacities encode how strongly a pixel prefers a label and how similar neighbours are. The minimum cut then splits the pixels into foreground and background in the way that best respects those preferences, cutting the fewest and cheapest connections.

Cut equals decision:

In segmentation, the min cut literally is the answer: the edges it cuts define the boundary between foreground and background pixels.
This turns a fuzzy vision task into a precise optimisation: find the cut that best balances each pixel own preference against agreeing with its neighbours.
Because the min cut is exact and efficient, segmentation by graph cuts became a standard technique in computer vision.

items: Each pixel is a node
Edges to source and sink encode label preference
Edges between neighbours encode similarity
The min cut is the best foreground background split

blocks.text: Another elegant use is the project selection or maximum closure problem. You have projects with profits and prerequisites, and you want to pick a set that maximises total profit while respecting dependencies.

By modeling profits and dependencies as capacities into a source and sink, the minimum cut corresponds to the optimal choice of which projects to take and which to skip. A profit maximisation problem becomes a cut minimisation problem.

items: Projects have profits and prerequisite dependencies
Model them as a flow network with a source and sink
The minimum cut selects the optimal profitable set
A maximisation problem solved by a minimum cut

blocks.text: The trick is wiring profits to the source and costs or prerequisites to the sink, so that cutting the network cheaply corresponds to the most profitable feasible selection.
It is a lovely example of turning a business decision into a graph cut.
The max flow min cut relationship shows up across many connectivity and partition problems.

items: Edge connectivity: the fewest edges whose removal disconnects two nodes
Vertex connectivity, by splitting nodes to turn them into edges
Baseball elimination, deciding if a team can still win
Bipartite matching, where the min cut explains the matching size

blocks.text: In each, the min cut identifies the true bottleneck, whether that is a set of edges, a set of nodes, or a set of decisions.
The unifying idea across all of these is that a minimum cut identifies the tightest barrier, whether the barrier is edges, nodes, or a set of choices.
Once you learn to see barriers as cuts, a whole class of problems becomes solvable with one tool.
This is why max flow min cut is considered a modeling superpower rather than just a single algorithm.
Finding the min cut costs essentially the same as finding the max flow, plus one cheap traversal.

items: Compute the max flow first, for example with Edmonds-Karp in O(V times E squared)
Then one search over the residual graph, O(V plus E), finds the cut
So the min cut is found for free once the flow is known
Faster max flow algorithms like Dinic carry over directly

blocks.text: Because the cut comes almost for free after the flow, any improvement to the max flow step immediately speeds up finding the min cut.

The cut is a bonus:

Since the min cut comes from one extra traversal after the flow, it is essentially free. Any faster max flow algorithm speeds up the cut too.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: Keep these points in mind when using the theorem.

items: The min cut counts only forward crossing edges, using the original capacities, not residual ones
Find the reachable set in the residual graph after the flow is maximised, not before
Model node capacities and node removals by splitting nodes into an in and out pair
The real skill is recognising a problem as a cut, just as with max flow

blocks.text:
Think in cuts:

Many optimisation problems are secretly asking for a minimum cut. If a problem is about the cheapest way to separate two things, max flow min cut is likely the tool.
The recurring lesson is that implementation is the easy part. The craft is modeling a problem so that its answer is a maximum flow or a minimum cut in the first place.
Max flow min cut ties together sending the most and severing the least into one theorem.

items: A cut splits the nodes into a source side and a sink side
A cut capacity sums the forward edges crossing it
The maximum flow equals the minimum cut capacity
The min cut is found from the residual graph after computing max flow
It solves segmentation, project selection, connectivity, and matching

blocks.text: Whenever a problem asks for the cheapest way to separate a source from a sink, remember that the answer equals the maximum flow, and the residual graph hands you the cut itself.
Hold on to the image of a dividing line: the most you can flow across it equals the least capacity you must cut to close it, and the residual graph shows you exactly where that line is.
